transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-02
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alice Johnson (Redwood AE), Ben Tran (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (CTO, Atlas), Derek Wu (Eng Lead), Nina Patel (Infra), Rahul (ML Eng)

Summary: SE (Ben) leads runtime tuning session. Focus on continuous batching, scheduler parameters (max_num_seqs, max_tokens, priority fairness), and interactions with KV cache + quantized weight paths in on-prem VPC setups. Customer interested in lowering p99 latency while improving throughput for 512-token workloads.

---- Auto-generated sections (may be noisy) ----
Topics: throughput tuning, KV cache warmup, quantization tradeoffs
Action items: see notes below

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alice Johnson: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, we've got 55 minutes on the calendar, we'll let Ben take most of the deep dive today.
[00:12] Ben Tran: hey all, yep I'll jump in — quick agenda: explain continuous batching, go through scheduler knobs, talk about max_num_seqs and token limits, then KV cache behavior with quantized models and finally ops considerations for VPC/on-prem. Sound good?
[00:22] Maria Lopez: yep, that's perfect. We mostly care about throughput on our on-prem clusters, plus latency SLOs at p95/p99.
[00:30] Derek Wu: and we want to make sure whatever tuning you recommend won't blow up memory or break other tenants.
[00:36] Ben Tran: totally. quick note — I'll reference the tuning spreadsheet I'm about to share, link in chat: https://redwood.example.com/tuning/atlas-staging-spreadsheet (note: this is a sample link)
[00:50] Nina Patel: received, thanks. small thing: our models are quantized to q4_0 and we run on A300-ish nodes, 40GB. we've seen KV cache thrash when sequences hit 2k tokens.
[01:05] Ben Tran: right, that aligns with known behavior — when token lengths vary a lot, the KV cache warming causes spikes. continuous batching can smooth that but requires right scheduler settings.
[01:18] Rahul: quick question — is continuous batching safe with stateful chat sessions? we want to keep prefix caching but still batch effectively.
[01:26] Ben Tran: yes, continuous batching in Redwood's runtime keeps KV cache per session — it does prefix caching and preserves KV entries per session id. you get batching across independent sessions but we avoid cross-session KV mixing. small transcript note: sometimes the auto-transcriber shows 'K-V cash' instead of 'KV cache'.
[01:40] Speaker 6: (inaudible)
[01:45] Ben Tran: so first concept: max_num_seqs — this is the maximum number of sequences the scheduler will coalesce into a batch for decoding. default is 16 in our hosted profiles but on-prem you might bump to 32 for higher throughput as long as memory allows.
[01:59] Derek Wu: memory is our limiter. at 32 sequences with 512 tokens we see memory bump, do you recommend also limiting max_decode_tokens?
[02:09] Ben Tran: yes, you can cap per-request tokens (max_decode_tokens) — so for requests we often set max_decode_tokens to 512 for interactive workloads; combined with max_num_seqs gives you an upper bound on memory. also there's a scheduler knob max_concurrent_batches which controls how many in-flight batches per worker.
[02:26] Maria Lopez: and what's the tradeoff for increasing max_num_seqs? latency vs throughput?
[02:31] Ben Tran: exactly — higher max_num_seqs increases throughput (more tokens/second) but increases tail latency because a request might wait longer till batch fills or the deadline. continuous batching has a per-batch deadline (batch_timeout_ms) to bound latency. we recommend starting with batch_timeout_ms = 20-30ms for sub-200ms p95.
[02:50] Nina Patel: our p99 is spiking to 1.2s on longer contexts — is that mostly due to KV cache misses or something else?
[02:57] Ben Tran: often it's KV cache thrash plus model loading/quantization kernel fallbacks. if your q4 kernel sometimes falls to a slower path for certain ops, you'll see jitter. check the runtime logs for kernel fallback entries.
[03:12] Rahul: what's kernel fallback?
[03:14] Ben Tran: when a specific op isn't supported in the fast quantized kernel, the runtime runs a slower reference kernel. that shows up as per-batch anomalies. Ben: we will share a log grep pattern for that.
[03:23] Alice Johnson: quick interjection — one operational lever is to reserve a small pool of fast workers (dedicated) for low-latency endpoints and leave the rest for high-throughput background jobs.
[03:35] Derek Wu: we do have dedicated pools in staging, yeah. how do we prevent starvation?
[03:40] Ben Tran: use priority routing and preemption thresholds. Redwood's scheduler supports priority_classes where you give latency-sensitive routes higher priority and a preemption cushion percentage.
[03:50] Maria Lopez: can you walk through an example config?
[03:52] Ben Tran: sure. example: 
- max_num_seqs: 24
- batch_timeout_ms: 25
- max_concurrent_batches: 4
- max_decode_tokens per request: 512
- priority_class: interactive with reserve 20% of GPUs
These numbers are starting points — memory and model size will push them down.
[04:22] Nina Patel: about batch_timeout_ms, if we set it too low we lose batching efficiency, too high we blow latency — any heuristic?
[04:30] Ben Tran: heuristic: target median queue length of 8-12 sequences; measure queuing delay and token throughput. If average queueing delay exceeds 12ms increase batch_timeout to 40ms. If p95 latency is increasing more than throughput gains, lower max_num_seqs or reduce batch_timeout.
[04:48] Speaker 6: uh-huh
[04:50] Ben Tran: next: token limits and truncation policies — decide if you want to truncate the prefix (LIFO) or drop oldest tokens (FIFO) when hitting context window. for HealthTech compliance you might prefer to retain recent context, so LIFO truncation is typical.
[05:07] Maria Lopez: yep we need last-24h context, but it's ok to drop older conversational history.
[05:12] Ben Tran: good. on KV cache behavior: cache warming matters — if you have many short-lived sessions the cache hit rate will be low. we advise a small warmup policy: pre-allocate KV cache entries for sessions expected to be reused, or use a sticky routing to keep session affinity on the same worker.
[05:29] Derek Wu: sticky routing might reduce utilization though.
[05:31] Ben Tran: tradeoff: stickiness improves cache hit rate and latency, but can fragment capacity. often a hybrid works: stickiness for VIP customers; otherwise round-robin.
[05:40] Nina Patel: quantization question — our q4 model produces slightly lower quality on branch predictions, any tuning tips?
[05:46] Ben Tran: if quality drop is visible, try PTQ calibration with an evaluation set, or hybrid quant: keep last layers in fp16 and quantize bulk to q4. also experiment with per-channel vs per-tensor quantization; we'll share recommended calibration commands.
[06:02] Rahul: will changing quantization settings affect KV cache size?
[06:06] Ben Tran: yes, some quant formats store different KV value shapes — generally smaller quant reduces KV memory; but per-kernel micro-ops can change so monitor both compute and KV memory.
[06:17] Maria Lopez: we're using a VPC with on-prem control plane, any network considerations for KV cache warmstart or shared baseline?
[06:24] Ben Tran: for on-prem, ensure low-latency interconnect between workers (RDMA if available). avoid remote KV fetches across regions. Redwood's private deployment can be configured to keep KV cache local to worker; if you enable distributed KV you'll want a fast local fabric.
[06:40] Derek Wu: what about auto-scaling — burst capacity tends to cause cold starts, right?
[06:45] Ben Tran: correct. if you scale up quickly new workers have cold KV caches and model warming cost. recommended approach: keep a small buffer of warm standby instances and prefer vertical scaling (more GPUs per node) for predictable workloads.
[06:58] Nina Patel: can we pre-warm models on new workers?
[07:00] Ben Tran: yes — Redwood supports a pre-warm API call (start_model_warm) to load weights and optionally prime KV cache with synthetic prefixes. we'll share an example script.
[07:12] Speaker 6: (background)
[07:14] Ben Tran: ok moving on to scheduler diagnostics: important metrics to watch are queue_depth_histogram, batch_fill_time_ms, kernel_fallback_count, kv_hit_rate, and worker_memory_pressure. we'll attach a Grafana dashboard with the recommended panels.
[07:30] Maria Lopez: we saw kernel_fallback_count spikes last week, how to debug quickly?
[07:34] Ben Tran: grep for 'fallback' in runtime logs, and check the op name (e.g., matmul_transpose) — sometimes a fused op isn't supported. short-term: increase batch_size to amortize cost; medium-term: update to runtime 2.4 which includes more kernels.
[07:49] Derek Wu: you're recommending an OS/runtime upgrade? downtime?
[07:52] Ben Tran: it's a rolling upgrade, no customer-facing downtime if you follow the canary steps in the ops guide. we'll share the canary playbook.
[08:00] Rahul: can we set different scheduler config per route? like chat vs batch?
[08:04] Ben Tran: yes, routes can have independent scheduler profiles. chat route can have lower max_num_seqs and smaller timeout to favor latency, while batch jobs get higher max_num_seqs.
[08:13] Maria Lopez: anything else about token limits we should know?
[08:15] Ben Tran: set per-route max_total_tokens to limit worst-case resource consumption; and consider per-customer rate limits. we also recommend request size normalization — for example map long single-token requests to streaming paths to avoid batching waiting on big requests.
[08:31] Nina Patel: how does streaming interact with continuous batching?
[08:34] Ben Tran: streaming is supported — the runtime can start streaming partial outputs while the batch completes. small caveat: streaming increases CPU overhead for response assembly; balance based on p95 latency goals.
[08:48] Speaker 6: hmm
[08:50] Ben Tran: now a concrete suggested config for Atlas staging (for 512-token median workloads):
- baseline workers: 8 nodes, 40GB GPUs
- max_num_seqs: 24
- batch_timeout_ms: 25
- max_concurrent_batches: 4
- warm_standby: 1 node
- prewarm_on_scaleup: true
- route profiles: chat (max_num_seqs 12, batch_timeout 18ms), batch (max_num_seqs 32, batch_timeout 50ms)

[09:30] Derek Wu: that sounds doable. what throughput increase can we expect?
[09:33] Ben Tran: ballpark 1.8-2.5x tokens/sec for interactive workloads vs conservative defaults. exact depends on your token distribution and q-kernel behavior.
[09:43] Maria Lopez: okay let's talk benchmark plan.
[09:45] Ben Tran: propose a 48-hour run on staging: 12-hour ramp, 24-hour steady, 12-hour ramp-down. collect queue metrics, kv_hit_rate, kernel_fallback_count, and p50/p95/p99 latencies. we'll provide the harness and expected queries.
[09:58] Nina Patel: we can do that. we'll need the harness and the dashboard.
[10:02] Alice Johnson: we'll share those, plus the tuning spreadsheet and our ops playbook.
[10:07] Rahul: any safety/security flags for on-prem? we have strict KMS policies.
[10:11] Ben Tran: Redwood Private integrates with customer KMS/HSM; for model warm-up scripts avoid logging sensitive prefixes in plain text — use hashed session ids in logs and route tokens to secure traces only. we'll include an ops-sec checklist.
[10:26] Maria Lopez: good. also, can you send the recommended scheduler ranges for our model sizes (1B, 6B)?
[10:32] Ben Tran: yes — smaller models can use higher max_num_seqs (32-48), larger models drop to 8-16. we'll put a sizing table in the doc.
[10:41] Derek Wu: any gotchas with autoscaling and quantized kernels?
[10:44] Ben Tran: autoscale can cause kernel mismatch if you upgrade runtime versions mid-scale; keep runtime consistent and use rolling upgrades. quantized kernels are stable but may require libcuda or driver versions that support faster int8 ops. we'll list driver matrix.
[10:58] Speaker 6: (crosstalk)
[11:00] Alice Johnson: let's recap and confirm next steps.
[11:02] Ben Tran: recap: 1) Redwood to share tuning guide, dashboard link, sample harness; 2) Atlas to run 48-hour benchmark on staging with proposed config; 3) Redwood and Atlas to review results in follow-up call; 4) seeding fallback: reserve a dedicated small low-latency pool for critical routes.
[11:22] Maria Lopez: ok agreed. can you also include the kernel_fallback grep and the prewarm script?
[11:27] Ben Tran: yes will include both.
[11:29] Alice Johnson: I'll send the calendar invite for a follow-up the week after Nina's benchmark completes.
[11:35] Nina Patel: thanks everyone, we'll start provisioning today.
[11:40] Rahul: thanks, great session.
[11:42] Ben Tran: thanks all, bye.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-attributions in the auto-transcript (e.g., 'Speaker 6'), and minor OCR-like mistakes (K-V cash). The body includes real config examples and suggested heuristics.
